title: Engineering SNP Identity Panels for Psilocybe cubensis Cultivar Authentication: Biallelic and  Multi-Allelic Selection, Out-of-Sample Validation, Native Two-Cartridge Hyris bCUBE Deployment, and Cross-Species Specificity
content: Whole-genome variant data are now available for the major cultivars of Psilocybe cubensis, but routine cultivar authentication requires small, fixed, assay-ready marker sets. Here, I ask how much of the genome-wide population structure of 92 accessions can be captured by minimal panels, and whether lifting the customary biallelic filter improves the answer. The variant union (Psilocydia collection; reference MGC_Penvy_1, GCA_017499595.2) contains 1,063,997 distinct sites carrying 1,076,262 ALT allele records: 98.86% biallelic, 1.14% tri-allelic, 0.008% tetra-allelic. Under an identical benchmark—scaled Procrustes concordance with the genome-wide PCA, leave-one-out projection, repeated-split cross-validation, and multilocus-genotype resolution—I construct two 60-locus panels. The biallelic baseline (PS-60) attains in-sample Procrustes R² = 0.640 and leave-one-out R² = 0.447, with 56 unique multilocus genotypes and a largest identical-profile group of 22 accessions. Re-running selection without the biallelic restriction yields a panel dominated by tri-allelic loci (PMA-60; 58 tri-allelic, 2 biallelic), which are ≈26× enriched among the most informative candidate sites: in-sample R² = 0.993, LOO R² = 0.772, 73 unique genotypes, largest collision group 7, and zero loci shared with the biallelic panel. A panel-size sensitivity analysis identifies PMA-36 (the first 36 loci in selection order) as the cost-optimal configuration: cross-validated R² = 0.989 at 61% of full-panel typing cost, deployable as one sample per 36-well Hyris bCUBE cartridge using the four-channel optical configuration (FAM, HEX, ROX, Cy5); the full PMA-60 deploys on two cartridges, with the second cartridge adding 24 locus wells, eleven Module A replicate wells for in-run concordance QC, and a no-template control. Sixty assays were designed and verified in-silico (55 requiring short MGB-NFQ probes under three-way allele-Tm matching; amplicons 85–194 bp; all REF alleles verified against the reference assembly). In-silico genotyping of six non-cubensis Psilocybe genomes—including P. allenii and its sister species P. azurescens—shows that neither panel cross-amplifies outside P. cubensis: zero directly transferable assays in any species, for both the biallelic (0 of 360 species–locus combinations) and multi-allelic (0 of 216) designs. Plotting the geographic origins claimed by cultivar trade names against the genotypic clusters shows that names are not records of provenance in this species: accessions claiming three continents share a single multilocus genotype, and single trade names recur in genetically distant clusters—the signature of clandestine rebranding, resolvable by genotyping rather than naming. Locus identities, allele states, per-sample genotypes and assay oligos of the multi-allelic panel are withheld under licence; a salted SHA-256 commitment to the full locus specification is published to establish priority without disclosure.
